title: Preface

teacherSummary.text: The 1818 Preface (written by Percy Shelley in Mary's voice) claims the central event is not impossible according to some physiologists, insists the story aims to show 'the amiableness of domestic affection,' and recalls the ghost-story origin.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Preface,” how does Shelley show the author's stated purpose? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the tone / mood you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Preface, how does Shelley develop the idea of the author's stated purpose? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the tone / mood in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Preface develops the idea of the author's stated purpose. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of tone / mood and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Preface (where it begins, turns and ends) and its tone / mood shape the reader's understanding of the author's stated purpose. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Preface suggests about the author's stated purpose. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's tone / mood and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses tone / mood in Preface to complicate the reader's understanding of the author's stated purpose. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Preface within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the author's stated purpose responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Preface alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the author's stated purpose follows or bends those conventions, using the tone / mood as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Preface and its treatment of the author's stated purpose. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's tone / mood and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Preface as evidence for a larger claim about the author's stated purpose in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Preface as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the author's stated purpose. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: The event on which this fiction is founded, has been supposed, by Dr. Darwin, and some of the physiological writers of Germany, as not of impossible occurrence. I shall not be supposed as according the remotest degree of serious faith to such an imagination; yet, in assuming it as the basis of a work of fancy, I have not considered myself as merely weaving a series of supernatural terrors. The event on which the interest of the story depends is exempt from the disadvantages of a mere tale of spectres or enchantment. It was recommended by the novelty of the situations which it develops; and, however impossible as a physical fact, affords a point of view to the imagination for the delineating of human passions more comprehensive and commanding than any which the ordinary relations of existing events can yield.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Preface”?
options: A privileged childhood and family love

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why might an author defend the 'possibility' of a fantastic event before the story begins? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are innovate, scrupled, spectres, environs, disadvantages. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “I have thus endeavoured to preserve the truth of the elementary principles of human nature, while I have not scrupled to innovate upon their combinations.” In this sentence it means: to make changes; to introduce something new. Word histories: “scrupled”: From Latin scrupulus "small sharp stone; uneasiness," the image of a pebble in one's shoe; the verb means "to hesitate on grounds of conscience." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Prefaces in the period often defended novels against charges of immorality or absurdity. Erasmus Darwin, mentioned here, was a well-known physician and poet who speculated about life. Why does this chapter matter? The Preface sets up the tension between scientific plausibility and moral fable that runs through the whole work. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for tone / mood.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “The event on which this fiction is founded, has been supposed, by Dr.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the author's stated purpose? I circle “spectres”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find tone / mood, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of tone / mood. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Tone / mood, Theme, Allusion: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Preface develops the idea of the author's stated purpose. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of tone / mood and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the author's stated purpose, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how tone / mood shapes the author's stated purpose. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
